Business.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
Business.text:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

"AI carries real risks," she added.

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

Business.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
Business.text:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.

But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."

Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.

Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.

Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.

And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

Business.title: Conservative media weighs its future as cracks emerge in Trump’s movement
Business.text:
As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy.

“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.

But two weeks on, Trump’s electoral wipeout is facilitating difficult conversations about the future of the conservative media ecosystem – and whether outlets that target a Republican-voting audience need to create some distance from an unpopular president. Some other outlets, like the Maga-aligned Real America’s Voice News network, are planning to go the other direction and double down on Trump.

“The whole landscape can now be reordered, and I think it will be,” said Steve Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump during his first administration who now hosts a show for Real America’s Voice.

Several conservative media personalities pinned the blame on Fox News for leading the party – and Trump – astray, with former host Tucker Carlson saying that the results signaled the end of “the Fox News era”. (Carlson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.)

Bannon, who contends that Rupert Murdoch has long “hated Trump”, predicted that the network will utilize the party’s recent “rejection” at the polls to move away from Trump and embrace more traditional, George W Bush-era Republican priorities.

“They’re going to try to kick Trump into the dustbin,” he said. “They clearly have moved beyond Trump and they want to move beyond Trumpism … What they’re going to do is, with a thousand cuts, convince their ageing audience that Maga and what Maga stands for is too extreme.”

In contrast, Bannon said he expects Real America’s Voice and other outlets to “triple down” on the Maga movement and “populist nationalism.”

Bannon is not alone in his criticism of Murdoch’s media empire. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter said that she views the channel and its sister outlet, the New York Post, as “90% responsible for the GOP wipeout in the midterm elections”, blaming voices in the Murdoch media empire for encouraging Trump to launch – and sustain – an unpopular war against Iran.

Atlanta-based conservative radio host Erick Erickson said a realignment away from Trump will probably start in his medium before it carries over to conservative television – though he said it will take time, and will depend on how important access is for certain personalities.

“The more often you spend time at Mar-a-Lago, the less likely you are to distance yourself from Trump, because you still want in,” said Erickson, who vocally opposed Trump in 2016 before coming around ahead of his 2020 re-election bid.

Charlie Sykes, a former conservative radio host who also opposed Trump from the beginning, said the election has shown “cracks in that alternative reality silo” on Trump-aligned channels and platforms.

“In general, I think the scope of the blowout was just so great that even deep in the rightwing media ecosystem, they had to feel the tremors of it,” said Sykes, a former MS Now commentator who now writes on Substack. “And so that has been kind of interesting, this sense of like, ‘OK, we need to really come to grips with this and maybe figure out a way to move on.’”

Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February fomented division within the conservative media ecosystem, with many commentators viewing it as an abdication of his promise to abstain from foreign wars and focus on the US.

“I think those divisions are just going to widen,” Sykes said.

The Daily Caller, which was co-founded by Carlson in 2010 as something of a conservative alternative to the New York Times, made waves ahead of the midterms for calling out Trump’s war against Iran – and the high prices that have come out of it. “The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post-Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intraparty media battle,” the digital publication Semafor wrote on 1 November.

In an interview, Daily Caller editor-in-chief Amber Duke said the publication is more focused on reflecting the mood of the American people – particularly younger people affected by a challenging economy – than boosting Trump and the Maga movement.

“I think what we are doing is so unique that we are really setting ourselves apart,” she said. “We view ourselves as a principled, America-first outlet. I think there’s a difference between Maga and America-first.”

Duke also acknowledged the economic opportunities that drive support for the president. “Trump is a content goldmine. He drives a lot of traffic, a lot of clicks,” she said. “That content mine is eventually going to dry up. I would definitely be concerned if I had my entire business model tied around this uniquely celebrity-oriented newsmaker. How am I going to continue to stay in business after that? For us, it’s: Let’s just tell the truth to the American people, and that truth is not going to be dependent on any one person or political party.”

Some conservative outlets that are closely tied to Trump, however, don’t see any reason to do anything differently.

“Nothing changes with us,” Newsmax chief executive Christopher Ruddy said. “We’re going to continue reporting on the administration and we will continue to cover the Congress. We make a very concerted effort to always get both sides on our reports and in our TV opinion segments.”

Charles Herring, president of the far-right One America News Network, echoed that sentiment: “Our reporting doesn’t change based on the political pendulum or who resides in the White House. We are working hard every day to further enhance our coverage for our viewers.”

Still, there are limits to how far some conservative media organizations can stray from the president, considering the economic imperative to retain a pro-Trump audience. “The thing to understand about conservative media is that it’s not necessarily always top down,” Sykes said. “It’s often: What will the audience tolerate? … Nobody wants to get too crosswise with their audience.”

But the vast majority of conservative news sites have already seen declines in online traffic in recent months, according to industry tracker Howard Polskin, an early warning sign for the party’s midterm chances. “Audiences are not buying what Maga media is selling anymore,” he said.

“My prediction would be that in the next two years, rightwing media will become fractured with more infighting, breaking into two camps: pro-Maga/Trump and anti-Maga/Trump,” Polskin added. “Traffic to rightwing websites will continue to nose dive, much more so than mainstream media.”

Several conservative media veterans who spoke with the Guardian said the selection of a 2028 Republican presidential nominee will probably be a defining moment for the sector, and one that could split conservative media into different camps.

On the notion that vice-president JD Vance will be Trump’s heir apparent, Erickson said: “I actually am kind of encouraged by the level of pushback after the election that maybe this isn’t a good idea.” Brian Kilmeade, the co-host of the influential Fox News morning show Fox & Friends, has been particularly critical of Vance for seeming to distance himself from Trump’s decision-making on Iran. On his radio show this past week, Kilmeade said that Vance “never should have been vice-president” and that he’s “amazed that President Trump puts up with it”.

Over the next two years, conservative media personalities will have to put their chips down on a candidate. The challenge, Sykes said, is “figuring out where the audience is going, and getting there first”. He also expects conservative media outlets to prioritize attacking Democrats and undermining their control of Congress.

“It’s no longer about defense of Trump,” he added. “It’s like: What’s next? And everybody’s got to make that pivot.”

Sports.text:
Alisson Becker: Caught one cross and took a few goal-kicks. Made a good save to deny Bruno Fernandes in stoppage time. Had little else to do. 6

Ronald Araujo: Never really tested defensively. Made a few contributions going forward. 7

Jeremy Jacquet: Went shoulder to shoulder with Bryan Mbeumo in the box at 0-0, although a penalty against the French defender would have been harsh. 6

Virgil van Dijk: Organised the defence well. Also had a header well-saved at 0-0 and nodded another wide in the second half. 7

Milos Kerkez: Always keen to drive Liverpool up the pitch. Had some nice link-ups with Rio Ngumoha. 7

Dominik Szoboszlai: Fantastic driven free-kick to open the scoring. Went close a few more times with long shots and generally bossed the midfield. 8

Alexis Mac Allister: Did all the simple things right and allowed others to shine around him. Forced Senne Lammens into a top save in the first half. 7

Bradley Barcola: Missed a few chances to score his first league goal for Liverpool when through one-vs-one. Showed his electric pace to set up his side's third. 7

Florian Wirtz: Readjusted well to net Liverpool's second and assisted their fourth. Five goals in four games for club and country now and looks close to his creative best. 8

Rio Ngumoha: So direct and skilful. Scored Liverpool's third with a calm finish. Also set up their second after easily beating Diogo Dalot. Club and country have a real talent on their hands. 9

Alexander Isak: Led the line well but missed some big chances. Won the free-kick that resulted in Szoboszlai's goal and led to Leny Yoro's sending off. 6

Victor Munoz (on 72, Barcola): Good cameo and took his goal well, curling it into the far corner. 7

Trey Nyoni (on 72, Mac Allister): Looked bright. Had a shot go just over. 6

Jeremie Frimpong (on 78, Ngumoha): 5

Joe Gomez (on 85, Araujo) 5

Lewis Koumas (on 85, Isak) 5

Subs not used: Chiesa, Mamardashvili, McConell, Tsimikas.

Senne Lammens: Could he have done better with the opener? Good save to deny Mac Allister and some decent stops after that. 6

Leny Yoro: Did he have to make the tackle on Isak? It was almost as though he thought about whether he should and decided the answer was yes. Given Liverpool scored from the free-kick it was a bad decision. 4

Matthijs de Ligt: First Premier League start in almost 12 months in middle of a back three turned into a nightmare with the early error that led to opening goal and Yoro red card. Struggled from that moment on. 4

Lisandro Martinez: Fully extended by Liverpool's attack. The least bad of the visitors' starting defence, but that isn't saying much. Exposed completely by Barcola for Liverpool's third. 5

Diogo Dalot: Given a torrid time by Ngumoha, which prompted Pochettino to bring on Maguire. Tries hard but it's not enough. 5

Youri Tielemans: Concerns about a midfield partnership with Mainoo emerge again. Not having the sustained impact required for a player of his experience. 4

Kobbie Mainoo: Twenty-one-year-old being asked to shoulder so much responsibility in an ailing team. New midfield recruits have not helped him. 5

Bryan Mbeumo: Couple of decent bursts came to nothing, then sacrificed after Yoro red card. Received consoling pat on the head from his new boss. 5

Bruno Fernandes: Early free-kick just wide and shot straight at Alisson. Given the carnage at Old Trafford this season, no wonder contract talks on hold. Furious at free-kick given against him when he thought he was through. 5

Patrick Dorgu: Asked to do an awful lot, initially as wing-back, then further back. Lucky Barcola fluffed his lines or his failure to keep an offside line would have been exposed. 5

Matheus Cunha: Tried to keep simmering frustration in check. Not easy in a losing side with no service. Replaced at the break. 5

Harry Maguire (on 22, Mbeumo): Couldn't have expected to be called on so soon. Went into middle of back three and immediately blocked an Isak effort to prevent a third goal. Tried hard. 5

Sports.title: Liverpool vs Man Utd: Was red card for Leny Yoro in Premier League the correct decision?
Sports.text:
Leny Yoro's eighth-minute red card was a pivotal moment early in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United boss.

It handed Liverpool the initiative at Anfield, and Andoni Iraola's players took advantage by scoring two goals in quick succession.

Should it have been a red card though?

Was there a case for the video assistant referee (VAR) to suggest it should be downgraded to a yellow?

Let's take a look at the incident, and what a referee takes into account before showing a red for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

Ronald Araujo played a long ball upfield for Alexander Isak to run on to.

Isak took a touch, before Yoro bundled into the back of the Sweden international and brought him down.

Referee Sam Barrott did not hesitate, giving the foul and sending off Yoro.

Was there doubt that Isak would have taken control of the ball? If so, it should only be a caution.

There are four key considerations for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity:

distance between the offence and the goal

general direction of play

likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball

location and number of defenders and attackers

As Isak was running directly towards goal in a central position, and there was no covering defender, three of the factors were satisfied.

The question is about the "likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball".

The Liverpool striker took a heavy touch, which moved the ball a few yards ahead of him.

The touch came before contact from Yoro, so there is no case that the challenge caused Isak to over-run the ball.

The referee and the VAR, John Brooks, must therefore assess whether Isak would definitely have got to the ball ahead of Senne Lammens. And that if he had, it would have been a good scoring chance.

If there is any doubt, then it should not be a red card.

It is a borderline case, and as such the VAR would not be expected to intervene for a clear and obvious error.

Likewise, if the referee had shown a yellow the VAR would not get involved.

Former Liverpool and England midfielder Danny Murphy, who is a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said there was "no doubt" about the red card.

Former Manchester United defender Gary Neville also agreed with the decision.

"Leny Yoro has to cover and he doesn't," Neville said on Sky Sports. "He reacts late and his anticipation is poor.

"It's so clumsy from Yoro. It's naivety, he just needs to get off the pitch. You're not going to get that turned around, no chance."

Sports.title: Hull City 2-0 Brighton: Keeper Konstantinos Tzolakis stars for Tigers after Greece nightmare
Sports.text:
Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic used one word to describe the performance of his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis in Sunday's 2-0 Premier League win against Brighton.

"Unbelievable," he told Match of the Day.

"Especially after the international break, which was very difficult for him."

Tzolakis' previous outing had been for Greece against the Netherlands in the Uefa Nations League, where he and his side were humbled 7-0 by the hosts in Amsterdam.

Nine days later, his contribution to the Tigers' first league victory since 29 August was every bit as important as that of striker Oli McBurnie, who netted both goals in second-half stoppage time against the second-placed Seagulls.

Tzolakis made a series of top saves to keep the highest scorers in the top flight at bay and, when Brighton full-back Costinha was sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, the hosts seized their opportunity to clinch only their third win following their Premier League return.

McBurnie said the 24-year-old stopper had "kept Hull in a few games" this season and the club were "lucky to have him", while Tzolakis told Sky Sports: "We are a unit and a team.

"We play for each other. We showed a good team effort and we deserved the three points."

With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported £20m fee.

He got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.

Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.

Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.

Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, said: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time.

"When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day.

"It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'."

Sports.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: Max Verstappen the constant amid chaos as he takes revenge on George Russell
Sports.text:
Warning: This article contains offensive language

Max Verstappen was a constant amid the chaos at a remarkable Las Vegas Grand Prix.

He was the star figure in a race that had 34 overtaking moves for the lead in 50 laps and 352 overall, in which the biggest advantage the leader ever had was 1.5 seconds, and in which there were five cars fighting nose to tail for the lead to the final lap, and for much of the race many more than that.

Even better for Verstappen, George Russell made a critical mistake 24 hours after he had revived his long-standing, on-off spat with the Dutchman.

Russell, who had been Verstappen's main threat from the start of the race, locked up his brakes and speared into the barrier trying to pass Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli for second place behind Verstappen with two laps to go.

Verstappen said: "He speaks a lot next to the track, and it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, you know?

"And today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening. I was, like, "Fantastic, my day is only getting better."

"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Verstappen felt motivated to make these remarks because of what Russell had said the day before.

After an on-track altercation in practice, the pair had had an exchange of views in the stewards' room. Then, after Verstappen took pole from Russell - after fastest man Antonelli's five-place penalty was taken into account - the Briton took a pop at the Dutchman.

"I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else," Russell said. "Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

In the paddock, a number of people felt that Verstappen was probably not the right "guy" to pick a fight with.

Even though Russell was battling with Verstappen throughout the race, the nature of their drives was different.

Russell would pass the Red Bull on the straight. Then Verstappen would reclaim the lead in more extreme fashion, on the outside of the fast kink leading on to the pit straight, or on the outside again at the long Turn Three.

Hardly anyone else even tried these moves, let alone pulled them off. Verstappen made them look routine.

After his error, Russell managed to extricate himself from the crash barrier, but he had turned a certain podium finish into a ninth place.

It was the perfect encapsulation of a season in which almost nothing has gone right.

For Verstappen, it was almost too good to be true.

The race was unlike any grand prix anyone younger than about 70 had ever seen.

The fabled slipstreaming battles of a pre-chicane Monza in the 1960s and early 1970s - that led to the closest ever finish in F1 history at the 1971 Italian Grand Prix,, external when the first five cars crossed the line 0.6secs apart - were the closest comparison at the highest echelon of the sport.

In modern terms, it was more reminiscent of American oval racing, where the high-speed nature of the race tracks leads to long chains of cars slipstreaming and lots of overtaking, little of it meaningful until the final stages.

Mercedes F1 team boss Toto Wolff pretty much hit the nail on the head when he said: "It was Indy 500 and Nascar and Formula 1 mixed - I enjoyed it."

And it encapsulated something else about F1 2026 - the internal debate that has been raging in the sport about artificiality ever since the latest engines were introduced.

The near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power has created energy-starved cars where the batteries run out before the end of long straights.

On certain tracks this has led to a form of racing known as "yo-yo", where cars constantly pass and re-pass each other depending on their respective levels of battery charge.

After a chaotic few races early in the year, this has diminished as teams have better understood energy management.

But in Las Vegas the combination of long straights and slipstreaming brought it to its apotheosis. And no-one quite knew what to think about it.

Verstappen said: "Really, really surreal and something that I've never seen before in Formula 1 myself.

"It was just a crazy amount of fighting. The slipstream was so big that you - it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were just following you.

"It was just very exciting, I guess, for everyone to watch. I know, of course, it's a big show around here the whole weekend, and I hope that we delivered on track."

That was a carefully judged answer for the television cameras, the sort that sounds like one thing, but if you know the person's real views, you can read between the lines to see the nuances that hint at something else.

In the news conference, Verstappen's true feelings came out. Was it a kind of racing he enjoyed?

"When I look at it from my racer heart, not," he said. "When you look at it as a show spectacle, yes.

"I enjoyed my repassing and everything, but I prefer to look at it with my racing heart. Even my heart rate, I was not nervous at all because it's just felt kind of cruising out there, just trying to press the battery whenever it was correct or defend.

"But for the show, when you look at it from the outside, probably, yes, you like it. But, yeah, I don't know.

"I probably shouldn't say it. I probably should not. I remember winning one like this when I was playing Mario Kart.

"Sometimes you drop back and you get drafts, and there's like a catch-up, you know? Always when you're dropping back, you go faster. So that's the last time that I felt something like this."

Other drivers said similar things.

McLaren's Lando Norris, who finished second, said: "From a racing point of view, from the outside, I'm sure it probably was the best race ever in Formula 1.

"You never know what's going to happen. There were overtakes out of nowhere, and some of the overtakes weren't overtakes, you press boost and you go past someone. But the racing was still good. You're still fighting for position, and there are a lot of good things in there."

Russell said: "It was interesting. It was quite fun for maybe half the race, but then it started to get a bit tiring at one point because it was just absolutely impossible to get away."

Essentially, this is an argument between racing purists and casual fans, especially the new ones who know little of the complexities of the sport. Wolff related a story about his wife Susie's experience with corporate guests during the race.

"I guess you will have many people that will say that's not racing," Wolff said. "Personally, we need to be open minded.

"Susie was in the Paddock Club and she said that for 90 minutes people were screaming with the overtakes.

"The instant feedback I got from the friends watching, our sponsors, was that was awesome. Stefano [Domenicali, the F1 chairman] liked it very much. That's not going to happen everywhere."

Verstappen's Mario Kart comparison brought back memories of his criticisms of the new F1 in the first few races, when he said he hated it so much he was considering stopping.

Since then, the current rules have been tweaked, and more changes have been introduced for 2027 and 2028 to reduce this effect.

And, irony of ironies, this weekend it was announced that there will be new rules for 2030. These retain turbo hybrid engines but reduce the electrical element, with the express intention of removing energy starvation and making racing 'pure' again. The likely result will be that this kind of race could not be possible again after that.

In the context of Vegas, is this actually a mistake?

Wolff said: "We're still doing the right thing. It's what we all wanted. But I have no doubt people will complain there is not great overtaking. We go back to the 'glorious years' in the 2000s. But we're gonna get those regs right. We see what we can do. It just needs a kilometre and a half straight."

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella added: "It's very difficult to have a position as simple as saying, 'Oh, that's the race we want.' Because as soon as you say that, you will see some other perspectives which are important to consider.

"Like, I still have to talk to Lando and Oscar (Piastri) and understand, did you enjoy it or that was kind of too much and at times it felt like this is going to go very wrong from a safety point of view?

"So, I don't want to express a net position. Because, in fact, I don't have it.

"This race gave us a lot of information that we cannot ignore. In terms of the attention, the spectacle, in terms of, you know, like, wow, that's incredible racing, is this what we want?

"My main recommendation is that we remain kind of analytical. And we remain caring for the interest of the sport.

"Because we live in a world where everything is polarised, a world in which you need to have an opinion in one second. Otherwise you are a nobody. You need to have an opinion that is polarised.

"Well, I would like to have people that actually still value complexity of analysis. And caring for a common interest. That's my main message.

"When you have examples like today which offer so much information it would be a shame to process it in the space of a hot review. And say, 'Oh, let's abandon the new regulations.' That's not the case.

"But definitely there's some interesting information that we should consider from a technical point of view, from a sport regulation point of view."

Sports.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face tense discussion over ability to race together
Sports.text:
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face yet another tense discussion over their ability to race together cleanly on track after colliding in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc tipped Hamilton into a spin with 22 laps to go, costing both points in a race where at one stage they were racing with the McLarens, who finished on the podium.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, which meant he finished 10th, three places behind Hamilton, in a race won by Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

It was the second race-compromising incident within three grands prix, and it came after the drivers had been brought together to clear the air at the last race in Brazil after their first-lap fighting in Mexico cost them a win.

Hamilton said such an incident "should never happen" but added that: "The question should be for Ferrari now."

Leclerc said: "We just need to fix whatever is not working."

Team principal Frederic Vasseur described the situation as "completely unacceptable".

The Frenchman said: "It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsor, the same speech as after Mexico.

"We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you're passed by others. It means you have to do your race and Charles clearly made a mistake.

"It's penalising the team a lot and it's completely unacceptable. Honestly we are more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico, we had a chat together in Brazil, today we passed the message to think about the team when racing together and the outcome is this one."

The battle between the two drivers has been tense all season, and in the second part of the year there have been a series of flashpoints, whether it be on-track racing, disputes about how best to work through strategy, and Hamilton ignoring two separate calls to pit in different races, both of which compromised his result, because he was looking at beating Leclerc.

Hamilton said: "It's not something I want to really get into."

The seven-time champion, who struggled against Leclerc last year but who has been revived in 2026, deflected questions about whether he should be given number-one status.

"I've never asked to be number one," he said. "I genuinely haven't ever asked.

"There was a point in the season where I was 40-odd points ahead, and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi (Antonelli).

"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year.

"At that point, we needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few instances in the season where, with the support, I think we could have beaten Kimi.

"But no, that's not what I've asked for. We shouldn't have gotten together. That should just never happen. But I've said everything I can on it, and the question should be for Ferrari now."

Before the incident, the drivers expressed their differing views on team radio, Leclerc expressing his concern for the way Hamilton was defending, Hamilton saying they should be focused on catching the cars in front.

Leclerc said: "He needs to be careful with this squeezing because it's not going to end well."

Hamilton swore as he asked the team to tell Leclerc to "back off", adding: "I'm trying to catch these guys ahead."

This was similar to their different stances in Mexico, when Leclerc was attacking Hamilton on the first lap while the Briton felt they should be working together to defend their one-two positions.

Vasseur said he would talk to the drivers the day after the race, once the immediate heat of the situation had dissipated.

"You can't imagine the frustration for me, but more important for the guys at home," Vasseur said.

"I want to have a discussion tomorrow. Also, Charles to digest the situation. It's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race."

Leclerc said: "I don't think it's going to be intense. None of our discussions were intense, but surely it cannot continue like that.

"I've taken a penalty, so I guess the blame is on me from the stewards and I guess from the majority, so as a result I guess it was deserved."

Hamilton v Leclerc is turning into an unsolvable problem at Ferrari.

For the sake of the team's results, team principal Vasseur needs to find a way to get the two to race together on track in a way that does not constantly undermine the collective result.

McLaren have - mostly - managed it with Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

So far, Vasseur has been unable to, or his drivers have not allowed him to. Which explains his response to the latest incident in Las Vegas.

In this case, Vasseur is laying the blame squarely on Leclerc's shoulders. At other times, it has been more nuanced.

Even in Mexico two races ago, that was the case. Hamilton was claiming the moral high ground as the leader - he felt Leclerc should not have attacked him as he did on the opening lap.

But they are allowed to race, and it can also be argued that Hamilton had a share of the blame - had he braked a little earlier, he would have stayed on track, not lost position to Verstappen, and been the beneficiary as Leclerc was forced to hand back the place he had gained by cutting a corner.

Leclerc is in an unfamiliar position - he has always been faster than his team-mates in F1. Now, he finds himself alongside someone matching him.

Hamilton is not - he has had competitive team-mates before, and it has usually not ended well. Ask Fernando Alonso and Nico Rosberg about that.

There were "serious talks" between Hamilton and Leclerc, brokered by Vasseur, earlier this month to solve what Hamilton said were "big problems".

Both drivers said these were now behind them. Clearly they are not. Even when accepting he was at fault, there was a tone to Leclerc's remarks post-Vegas that made it clear he did not believe it was all entirely on him.

They are incredibly evenly matched, and both are determined to be the person who delivers the next title to Ferrari. Fighting like this could well mean neither does, even if the team are ever in a position to win one.

The immovable object meets the irresistible force. What's the solution to that equation?

Sports.title: Nations Championship: England will not get carried away by win against All Blacks - Matt Dawson
Sports.text:
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.

If England had produced that performance two years ago against New Zealand, there would have been a lap of honour and wild celebrations.

Saturday felt like business. Job done, move on. And that is how it should be.

It was a record victory for a northern hemisphere side against the All Blacks, yet at full-time you would hardly have known it.

Even the post-match messaging from their leaders - Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge and Steve Borthwick - was that this performance had always been in them and that nobody was surprised.

However, they will want to back it up.

A tired but hurting New Zealand side will arrive at Allianz Stadium next Saturday looking for revenge.

England beat the All Blacks in back-to-back Tests in 2002 and 2003. Matching that achievement on Saturday was a significant statement.

Three consecutive wins over New Zealand, followed by a third-place finish, would leave England in a strong position heading into 2027, when the Rugby World Cup takes place in Australia.

Lose, though, and it will be a waste of some great momentum.

We have had many a false dawn with Borthwick's England, but something feels different this time.

For me, that comes down to the players taking responsibility.

Many of us ex-pros called for it during the Six Nations, and finally we are seeing the players take the lead on the style of rugby they want to play.

It is an exciting, free-flowing brand of attacking rugby that mirrors what they are used to playing in the Prem.

England's backs can compete with the very best and they tore through New Zealand on multiple occasions.

Credit also has to go to Borthwick for allowing the players to take control. That, in itself, shows how he is learning and evolving as a head coach.

Once players start getting 40, 50, 60 or 70 caps, they know more about certain aspects of the game than the coach because they are the ones out there experiencing it.

If the environment does not allow players to turn around and say 'this isn't going to work', then it is never going to work.

The reports before the Australia game suggested honest conversations took place, with the players wanting a greater say in how the team operates.

The Six Nations was probably a big turning point. The change in mood and the feel-good factor are clear in the way England are carrying themselves.

They now feel in control and, crucially, have a genuine sense of ownership in shaping the team and how it plays.

Lewis Moody, a former team-mate of mine, joining the team to face the New Zealand haka was an enormous statement about English rugby.

Whether you are playing in 2026 or 1926, this is England rugby. We are together.

It was a united and extraordinary moment, one that will stay with me until the day I die. There was a clear bond as Lewis embraced every England player before leaving the pitch.

That was a huge driver for England. They were able to show their emotional vulnerability before quickly switching into game mode.

A record victory over New Zealand was so fitting for the occasion, but I am not getting overly carried away by the big scoreline.

The southern hemisphere teams are coming towards the end of a brutally long season. They have done a lot of travelling and played considerably more international rugby.

New Zealand and South Africa, in particular, had the added emotion of four summer Tests against each other in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series.

The Springboks also looked tired and strangely out of sorts in their defeat by Ireland.

At the beginning of the tournament, we were probably looking at it thinking it was a shame that the two top teams in the world were going to be on the same side of the draw.

Now, they have both lost back-to-back games, with injuries also playing a part.

England should not get carried away, by any stretch. It will be incredibly difficult for New Zealand to pick themselves up after that defeat.

The flight is waiting to take them home, they need some rest and will want to start thinking about next year's World Cup.

England, by contrast, will be chomping at the bit. They have momentum, and everybody is itching to get the white shirt on and run out at Allianz Stadium.

Saturday will provide another really good test of how England deal with being favourites. I expect changes to be made, but I still expect England to win.

After some difficult moments during this World Cup cycle, we are now seeing proper depth start to come through.

I can name at least two quality options in every position.

France will probably go into the final as favourites against South Africa.

Closing out back-to-back Six Nations titles and last week's victory over the world champions has given them the confidence to believe they can secure further silverware.

The Nations Championship has been a big success in replicating tournament rugby and, crucially, teaching teams how to win tight games.

Never write off the Springboks, but France are flying high after their performances against Argentina and South Africa.

Rassie Erasmus' side have lost back-to-back games, ending any perceived sense of invincibility. However, they only needed a point to reach the final and got that in Dublin.

Now it is winner takes all, and the world champions - with back-to-back Rugby World Cups and Rugby Championships behind them - should be in their element.

Fabien Galthie has rotated his squad tremendously well, and France will have more energy heading into next Sunday's final.

Those two points gained away to New Zealand with a second-string team in July ultimately proved decisive in the final standings.

I would have loved England to be competing for a trophy on this final weekend, but France have been the more consistent side.

The tables have turned, and suddenly the top teams in the world are in the northern hemisphere.

That is the magic of this new tournament. Everything can change in the space of a week.

Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Alastair Telfer.

Sports.title: Wales show signs of progress despite defeat by Australia, say Scrum V pundits
Sports.text:
For experienced hooker Ryan Elias, the proof of Wales' progress came when he looked around in the post-match huddle and saw heads down after a narrow defeat by Australia.

Steve Tandy's side failed to back up their historic victory against New Zealand when edged out 29-26 by the Wallabies in the Nations Championship.

Wales could not claim another scalp against the Aussies, who are two places above them in seventh in World Rugby's rankings, but they went close.

"It wasn't that long ago, not even 12 months ago, that we probably would have been chuffed with that result," said 54-cap forward Elias.

"You look around the circle at the end of that game and there were boys with heads down because this is one that got away.

"That just shows the growth of the group and the belief that's coming."

Next Sunday is the one-year anniversary of Wales' 73-0 defeat by South Africa in Cardiff, a hammering that was followed by heavy Six Nations losses against England and France.

Tandy's squad have since enjoyed victories against Italy, Fiji and Japan before the statement success against New Zealand.

"It's hard to recreate what they did against the All Blacks," former Wales centre Tom Shanklin said on Scrum V podcast.

"It's hard to get to that level every week, but it was really positive. We're still in a building phase.

"We said the best thing about the Japan game was that it was a bonus-point win, and that was about it.

"That feels a long time ago. We've come a long, long way.

"The effort was there against Australia, but there just wasn't that clinical edge and maybe that's a psychological thing."

Wales were nervy 28-21 winners at the start of November against a Japan side who have since been thumped by England and Scotland.

They face the Brave Blossoms again on Saturday (13:10 GMT) at Nations Championship finals weekend at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

"This is a big game now to see how much we've changed and developed from the first game of the campaign to the last," said Shanklin.

Wales chalked up four-try bonuses in all three games in Cardiff and have added to their threat from driving line-out.

They have profited from consistency at 10-12-13 with Sam Costelow, Max Llewellyn and Eddie James.

"You're seeing a team that seems to have found an attack," said Shanklin.

"Matt Sherratt has worked really hard with them and we've got various options now, we're not too predictable.

"We're playing with a lot more quick ball and we're quite clever in how we're breaking teams down.

"There are multiple options now when taking the ball to the line and we are getting it into the hands of our strike runners."

Wales did, however, waste a number of 22 entries in the first half and the final try by Ryan Elias came after pressure that ate into the clock.

"We were really good up to about five or 10 metres out, then we lost the detail," said former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert on Scrum V.

"We didn't do a lot to get held up over the line. We were quite predictable around the corner and Australia won every physical battle and were very good defensively."

Louis Rees-Zammit vowed in the summer that he would fire during his second season back in rugby after his crack at the NFL.

The 6ft 2in wing has been true to his word and arguably the 2021 Lions tourist is a better player now than he was before heading to America in 2024.

Rees-Zammit provided more evidence of his pace and added power when creating Blair Murray's try down the right in the second half.

"I was in line with where Zam had the ball and thought that surely Harry Potter was not going to give him the outside," said Cuthbert.

"It was only three or four yards and he did a shimmy in and if he gets half a yard outside then he is so quick.

"But now he is so strong from the hip down, so broke through Potter and then [Joseph-Aukuso] Suaalii tried to come across and it looked like they got an arm on him.

"It's just that power and watch Rees-Zammit carry now and he makes yard after contact."

The Bristol back has returned to wing and Murray, one of Wales' star performers in 2024-25, has profited from starting at full-back.

"He's a class player isn't he?" said the Scarlets man about Rees-Zammit. "He is one of the best wingers in the world, and he shows it week in and week out.

"We're working well together, you know. Whether I'm putting him through holes or he's getting through and passing it back inside.

"That connection is growing and we want to get the ball in our hands as much as we can."

The pair and experienced wing Josh Adams look sure to start the Six Nations, fitness permitting.

Wales' win against the All Blacks gave a boost to ticket sales for the Wallabies fixture despite the late kick-off time.

The crowd of 66,307 was larger than the 52,425 against Japan and 55,152 against New Zealand.

Crucially, after the lows of last season's heavy defeats by South Africa and France, the connection seems strong between Tandy's team and the supporters.

"The atmosphere was amazing again," said Cuthbert, who scored two tries in the bedlam of the famous 2013 victory against England.

"You've got to give credit to the Principality Stadium staff, they are really making the place have that bit of theatre and entertainment."

Wales will hope it gives them an extra lift for the visits of Ireland and England in the Six Nations.

Sports.title: Liu Wenwei: Chinese snooker player suspended amid match-fixing investigation
Sports.text:
Chinese snooker player Liu Wenwei has been suspended from "attending or competing on the World Snooker Tour with immediate effect" amid an investigation into match-fixing.

The decision was announced on Sunday by World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA) chairman Jason Ferguson.

"This follows an investigation into him being a party to approaches made to players to fix matches and failing to report approaches made to him to fix matches on the World Snooker Tour," said a WPBSA statement., external

"At this stage, the investigation has not identified that any matches were fixed in this case.

"The suspension will remain in place until the conclusion of the investigation or any subsequent charges that may or may not be brought."

The 22-year-old Liu, who earned a two-year card on the World Snooker Tour starting with the 2025-26 season, has the right to appeal the decision.

Snooker increased its monitoring of match-fixing after their most high-profile case in 2023 led to 10 bans.

In an unrelated case to Liu, Liang Wenbo and Li Hang were given lifetime bans and eight others - including major winners Yan Bingtao and Zhao Xintong - were handed suspensions in 2023.

The allegations against the 10 players included manipulating games, approaching players to cheat, betting on snooker and fixing matches in 2022.

The cheating mainly revolved around fixing the scores, or the number of frames won in matches, with nine of the 10 players based in Sheffield.

WPBSA rules state that when it comes to approaches to fix matches, they should be reported "as soon as reasonably practicable and in any event not later than 24 hours after any such approach being made".

The rules add: "Further, the reporting member shall provide the WPBSA (via the Company Secretary or a Tournament Official) with all information in his or her knowledge relating to the approach and shall co-operate in any subsequent investigation and/or other action(s) arising out of such a report."

Sports.title: Marc Marquez wins MotoGP title: Record-equalling eighth for Spanish Ducati rider secured in Portugal
Sports.text:
Marc Marquez clinched a record-equalling eighth MotoGP championship with an eighth-placed finish in the Portuguese Grand Prix on Sunday.

The Spaniard needed to finish in the top nine on his Ducati to seal a second consecutive championship and move level with legendary Italian Giacomo Agostini on eight titles.

He started second on the grid and rode cautiously after crashing out in the sprint race on Saturday.

Aprilia's Italian rider Marco Bezzecchi, who held a 102-point advantage over Marquez at one stage this season, was Sunday's race winner, while Marquez's fellow Spaniards Jorge Martin and Raul Fernandez completed the top three.

But the attention was all centred around Marquez, who was hoisted in the air by his team after crossing the line.

The 33-year-old won seven grands prix and 10 sprint races this season, adding to the 11 grands prix he won in 2025.

While Sunday marked his eighth MotoGP title, it was Marquez's 10th championship overall after wins in the 125cc and Moto2 categories on his journey to the top.

Sports.title: Women's Super League: Spurs 'a match for anyone' as win at Man City boosts European dreams
Sports.text:
Dreams of reaching the Women's Champions League may have seemed fanciful for Tottenham Hotspur when the season began.

The Women's Super League has an established big four, and big-spending London City Lionesses were the side making the most obvious play to disrupt that dominance.

But a hugely impressive and deserved win at Manchester City on Sunday afternoon proves Spurs are a team on the up, and the table shows they remain firmly in top-three contention.

Two late goals secured a 3-1 win at Joie Stadium, but this was no smash-and-grab job. Spurs were more dynamic than sluggish City, pressing them into submission.

They restricted their hosts' stellar attack to precious few chances and took the ones they created.

"When we are on our game, we can be a match for anyone," Spurs manager Martin Ho said in his post-match media conference.

"It gives us confidence - but it is just one game."

Victory kept Spurs, whose highest finish in the WSL is fifth, firmly in the mix this time.

They are fifth again, but just three points behind London City Lionesses who occupy the final European place as the league heads into a last international break of 2026.

Chelsea lead the way from Manchester City, with Manchester United one point ahead of Tottenham, who in turn sit handily clear of their sixth-placed north London rivals Arsenal.

The big four are therefore all present in the top six. London City are right there, too, and Spurs, with six wins from 11 games so far, are gamely pressing their own case.

What made Sunday's win and performance from Tottenham even more impressive is how dreadful their recent record against Manchester City had been.

Tottenham had lost six of their previous seven away matches against City in all competitions, averaging over four goals conceded per defeat.

Last season City won this fixture 5-2 with Khadija Shaw scoring a 13-minute hat-trick, the quickest in WSL history.

Shaw's early goal on Sunday, her 16th in league matches versus Spurs, could easily have started a landslide.

That was expected. City had won each of their past 17 WSL home games, including all 10 in 2026 – until Tottenham tore up the script.

The outcome means Manchester City, beaten at Chelsea in their previous outing, have suffered consecutive league losses for the first time since January 2025.

Tottenham's victory came down to Ho's brave tactics and his team's superb execution of them.

After going behind, they pressed City constantly, forcing errors and creating chances. That tenacity won them countless one-on-ones, with City unable or unwilling to play over the press.

After her goal, Shaw was rendered anonymous by the hard work and close marking of centre-backs Toko Koga and Amanda Nilden.

Down the right, Kirsty Hanson dominated Carlotta Wamser, could have been awarded a penalty and provided the low cross for Cathinka Tandberg's equaliser.

In midfield, Drew Spence pulled all the strings and covered the entire pitch. At 34, she is perhaps playing the best football of her career and deserved her assist for the winner. After Matilda Vinberg put Spurs in front, several players ran to celebrate with Spence.

"When you come into this, you wonder if it will go against you, but the players were outstanding," said Ho.

"We haven't won here in so long, so we know it will be a tough game, but I have belief in my team when we are on song. I thought we were outstanding - we worked every blade of grass."

Spurs are clearly capable of taking the game to anyone in the league and have now scored 28 WSL goals this season, with only Chelsea and London City having more.

In the second half they adapted to City sending on such fluid attacking threats as Mary Fowler, Kerstin Casperij and Beth Mead.

They lifted the gas from the press, applying it more sparingly, and were solid in defence.

It shows that Ho has learned painful lessons from the past - whether from Spurs' poor record against City, including two five-goal losses in 2025-26, or conceding six to Chelsea and London City back to back in October.

"We have maybe been naive at times and I own that, so we are more reserved," Ho said of his tactical approach. "It was managing that, and the players' communication was excellent."

City were limited to fleeting chances. Jade Rose blasting over after keeper Lize Kop parried a Lauren Hemp free-kick was as close as they came to a second goal, and those were their first shots after a 50-minute drought.

When Spurs got their late chances through the hard work of Vinberg, they could strike for three points.

Vinberg had quite the rollercoaster afternoon. She was initially named on the bench but was promoted to the starting XI 15 minutes before kick-off as Olivia Holdt was suffering stomach cramps.

Perhaps unprepared, she gave away the ball playing out of defence leading to City's opener. But she grew into the game, scored Spurs' second goal and set up Jess Naz for the third.

It was a great moment for Naz, on her 100th WSL appearance of a career that has been disrupted by injury.

Spurs are back in Manchester before Christmas, visiting United on 20 December.

There will be real hope of a positive result as they press their way into contention for what would be a historic achievement of a top-three finish.

Sports.title: Desire Doue injury: PSG forward to have surgery on ruptured ACL
Sports.text:
Paris St-Germain forward Desire Doue will have surgery later this month after rupturing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

The 21-year-old was in tears as he was taken off on a stretcher towards the end of the first half in the Ligue 1 champions' 3-2 victory over Nice on Saturday night.

Doue, who has arguably been PSG's best player this season, twisted awkwardly and went down under no contact.

The match was stopped for five minutes as Doue - who was visibly in pain - received treatment before he was applauded off by the crowd at the Allianz Riviera Stadium.

It is a huge set-back for the France attacker, who missed 13 games in 2025-26 with calf and hamstring injuries.

The European champions have been plagued with injury issues so far this season and are already without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, who sustained an ACL injury of his own against Barcelona in October.

PSG return to action on Wednesday, when they host Roma in the Champions League.

Sports.title: Liverpool hand Pochettino nightmare Manchester United start after Yoro sees red
Sports.text:
Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast-furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino’s debut descended into an ordeal after merely eight minutes when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after a comfortable, utterly dominant win peppered by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai, Victor Muñoz and the two creative forces. “Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic day in the job.

The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who only met his new charges on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake, and one that contained destructive repercussions for the entire United team and their performance.

That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia himself but his replacement at centre-half was heavily responsible for the chaos that unfolded. The Netherlands international was ultimately at fault for three goals. Liverpool, under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the mishaps in the visitors’ central defence.

De Ligt lost both the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger unfolding around his fellow centre-half. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save him. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.

A simple detail showed the extent of the job that Pochettino has on his hands: the United wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the stranded exception of Bruno Fernandes, there was no one covering the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.

Liverpool seized on the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United at Anfield did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha, starting on the left with Cody Gakpo out injured, tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.

The first chants of “Sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was of course a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.

Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead further. Lammens denied both and Maguire threw himself in the way of another Isak shot to deflect over.

Iraola must have had a word during the interval as Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from the £116m recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery from Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal that Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before rolling an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert at the back post.

Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the Champions League trip in Brugge in midweek and he made a triple substitution to rest players in the 72nd minute. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, enabled the hosts to pounce and Wirtz released Muñoz free inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do in the directors box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend, the actor James Nesbitt. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

Gaming_Tech.title: RAF's next fighter jet could be last crewed combat aircraft
Gaming_Tech.text:
Britain's next-generation fighter jet could be the last crewed combat aircraft the UK builds, the head of the RAF has said.

Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled, uncrewed aircraft would "transform military aviation".

His comments refer to the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a partnership between the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet, expected to enter service by 2035.

The aircraft, commonly known as Tempest, is expected to provide speed stealth, use advanced sensors and even AI to assist the human pilot when they are overwhelmed, or under extreme stress.

Writing in the Telegraph, external, Sir Harv said the GCAP aircraft was "perhaps the last crewed fighter we will ever build", not because people would become less important, but because advances in technology were changing the nature of air combat.

He said AI and machines would take on "the most dangerous tasks instead of humans", while stressing that technology should enhance human judgement and "not replace accountability". He added: "Uncrewed fighter jets will start flying in UK airspace next year. This is exciting and necessary in equal measure."

Sir Harv also said the RAF of the future would combine Typhoons and F-35s with autonomous systems.

The programme was announced in 2022 by the UK, Italy and Japan, which are jointly developing the aircraft. In July, the three countries signed a £4.6bn contract covering the next phase of its design through industry joint venture Edgewing.

According to GCAP, the aircraft will be powered by advanced data processing and artificial intelligence, while also featuring enhanced stealth technology. The UK government says the project already supports 3,500 jobs and 1,000 apprenticeships.

Canada was granted "observer nation" status in July, giving it privileged access to the programme without a decision-making role.

Gaming_Tech.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

Upstart says it is tackling that issue.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.
