EntertainmentTab.title: How Westside Cowboy went from student gigs to rising stars in two years
EntertainmentTab.text:
In two years, Westside Cowboy have rocketed from the sweaty corners of Manchester's student pub circuit to performances on one of America's biggest talk shows and at many of the UK's biggest festivals.

What started as jamming for fun in a student bedroom has become the latest revolution in British indie known as "Britainicana".

Now the quartet have been named the BBC Introducing Artist of the Year for 2026.

Westside Cowboy join a prestigious list that includes Myles Smith, Olivia Dean, Tom Grennan and several other now household names that have won the award.

But how did they get there, and so quickly?

It is 3 December 2024 and I am finally about to see Westside Cowboy.

A typical cold winter night on Oldham Street, Manchester, where four students are set to play their first headline show together in the innocuous backroom of a little pub called The Castle Hotel.

It was the launch night of their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You).

It is a sub-three-minute explosion of some of the finest pop rock you could ever hope to hear.

They had released the single on 7 November 2024 and uploaded it to the BBC Introducing website on the same day.

I played it on BBC Introducing on BBC Radio Lancashire that very night, and quickly forwarded it to the BBC Introducing Mixtape.

It was soon played by Emily Pilbeam on BBC Radio 6Music.

Westside Cowboy had the attention of the nation's music media.

By the time their second single Shells was released in April 2025, Westside Cowboy had been selected by BBC Introducing to play on their illustrious stage at Glastonbury festival.

The song also went straight on to the coveted 6Music playlist.

Every other single the band have released since has received the same treatment and more.

Paddy Murphy, Reuben Haycocks and Aoife Anson O'Connell met in autumn 2021 at the Royal Northern College of Music on Oxford Road.

One day, Murphy and Haycocks walked down Oxford Road to Johnny Roadhouse, a music shop fronted with an array of hanging brass instruments and full of Manchester folklore.

It has served the city's musicians since 1955.

They ran into guitar repairer, Jimmy Bradbury, who asked Murphy and Haycocks if they fancied starting a band called Westside Cowboy.

Be grateful that the answer was yes - with O'Connell joining later that evening.

Murphy and Bradbury had been in a band together before, a surf-rock trio called Katz, and Murphy and Haycocks both played in another trio, DieKaiDie.

Drummer Murphy played guitar for another band too, Holly Head, however O'Connell had not even played a guitar before she picked up the bass for Westside Cowboy. She was a cellist.

It is safe to say that this new band had plenty of competition for their time, but nevertheless it was soon to be their top priority.

It all began in Paddy's student bedroom.

Sessions where the modus operandi was shaking off the pretensions of their other perhaps more lofty-minded projects, and taking things back to basics to rediscover the answer to the question of why they actually loved playing music - because it was fun.

Within a few short months they were one of the country's hottest underground prospects, with videos of their live shows spreading all over Instagram.

On 1 February 2025 I introduced them on stage.

Westside Cowboy were one of four local artists showcased by BBC Introducing at The Grand in Clitheroe.

It was a set laden with songs they would release in the subsequent 18 months.

Then in April, I was calling them from our radio studio to tell them that they had been awarded one of the coveted spots on the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival 2025.

Westside Cowboy then also won Glastonbury's prestigious Emerging Talent Competition to perform on the Woodsies Stage alongside Blossoms and Scissor Sisters.

They were soon jetting off to New York to record their next EP with Loren Humphrey, whose reputation was soaring after the success of Heavy Metal - the debut solo album from Cameron Winter, the lead singer of Geese.

Westside Cowboy then headed to Paris for a 15-date European tour supporting their heroes, Black Country, New Road.

Their second EP was released in January 2026 titled So Much Country 'Till We Get There.

In the months that followed, Westside Cowboy were back touring Europe, this time opening for Geese, who had a decent claim for being the most exciting indie band in the world.

This was possibly the hottest support slot on the planet, and these four Manchester students had it.

They soon announced their own debut album It Goes On, which charted at No. 5 in the Official Album Charts.

The pinch-me moments weren't done with.

After a performance on Later… with Jools Holland on BBC Two, Westside Cowboy were off to America again to make their US television debut on The Tonight Show starring Jimmy Fallon, one of the most recognisable TV shows in the world.

It was still under two years since their first headline show.

In a world where artists fiddle frustratingly at algorithms trying to get their music to an audience on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and Spotify, this is an old school meteoric rise the likes of which the music industry must have thought no longer possible.

It has been achieved by four seemingly ordinary students regularly seen wandering down Oxford Road in Manchester.

Together the have been named the outstanding emerging act of the year by the BBC Introducing.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘He’s open and affable – I avoid being recognised like the plague’: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon on celebrity, friendship and their trip to the Arctic circle
EntertainmentTab.text:
Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it …”

The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker.

The pair are two weeks into filming series five of The Trip, the show devised by director Michael Winterbottom as a kind of blurry version of the actors’ real lives. Each season sends them on a kind of Epicurean road trip, under the guise of a journalistic commission; this time, the conceit is that Brydon is making a podcast for the Guardian, and Coogan has agreed to tag along.

Over the past 16 years, The Trip has taken them from the north of England to a meandering tour of Italy, via Spain and Greece. Now they have reached Scandinavia, heading through Sweden and Norway and up to the Arctic Circle, taking in luxury hotels, fishing huts, brown cheese and reindeer.

It has been six years since they last convened. Since then, much has happened in their lives. Brydon is an established national treasure, hosting gameshows and voicing Julia Donaldson adaptations, even writing a children’s book of his own. Coogan has combined a broad populism – revisiting his comic creation Alan Partridge and a turn in The White Lotus, with more nuanced projects – playing Jimmy Savile, for instance, and writing and producing Stephen Frears’s film The Lost King.

After breakfast, filming moves to the hotel spa, where Coogan and Brydon sit in bathrobes to record a podcast episode, their conversation drifting once again from saunas to birch twigs to an analysis of their own physiques. Meanwhile, the crew fold themselves into tight corners, hover behind camera lines, try not to laugh. All these years in, the show remains joyously funny. Still, in this quiet landscape it is hard not to notice the sense of contemplation that runs through this series; a rumination on age and friendship, pleasure, purpose, isolation and joy.

It is the following summer when we meet again: a wildly hot day in a central London hotel. By this stage, the series is finished, and Coogan has watched three episodes. “I was surprised at how much I laughed,” he says. “My memory was that it was just a bit haphazard and a bit silly, but different enough for it to be charming. What I wasn’t expecting was to find it so warm and welcoming. Throughout all the cynicism and arguments and spikiness, it has a real humanity.”

For a time they sit and discuss the moments that did not make the final cut: James Bond references, digs at other comedians, a plunge into a bracingly cold river. Some established elements of the show remain: there are the famed impressions, jabs about the directions of their respective careers, the appeal of light entertainment, the allure of politics, their differing relationships. But there are shifts in this series, too: subtle turns in subject matter, the old prickliness of their exchanges often giving way to a kind of tenderness.

They are keen, as ever, to differentiate between their onscreen relationship and a real-life friendship that has run for 30 years. These days, Brydon says the pair “get together and talk about middle-aged things”. Coogan nods. “We talk about things that are achingly middle-class preoccupations,” he says. “Things that are very, very unsympathetic.” He reels off a couple of examples: second homes, complaining about staff. “You see, when I was young and from a lower middle-class background, people used to laugh and joke and say: ‘Oh, you just can’t get the staff …’” he says. “And now I’m 60, and I’m in a different socioeconomic position, I do know what that means.”

Brydon looks up. “By the time this comes out, you’ll be 61,” he says. “It’s probably better to say 61. Let’s just say you’re mid-60s.”

Coogan frowns. “No,” he says. “Don’t say that.”

The matter of age runs through The Trip to the northern lights. Today, they talk about the subject with a kind of zeal. “What you notice is that thing of being a bit more carpe diem, a bit more living in the moment,” says Coogan. “Just trying to stand outside yourself, and celebrating if things are good.”

He noticed this growing feeling in his late 50s, though it only seemed to gather pace as he reached 60, and became a grandfather. “It’s a visceral, animal thing,” he says. “I’ve got a granddaughter, and I just want to see her, I just want to be with her, in a way that transcends all of the stuff. I want that almost like a child wants something.” He smiles. “Getting old is quite like being a child,” he says. “Children live in the moment, and they absorb, and they’re quite visceral. And I think when you get older, you start to do that too. I just want to do funny voices. And make her laugh and that’s enough.”

“What do you do for her, Neil Kinnock?” asks Brydon. “The wheels on the bus go round and round,” he sings in a recognisably Kinnockian intonation.

Coogan nods. “Yes,” he says. “Just because I know that when she gets older and she starts asking, what does it mean: ‘Hiring taxis to scuttle around handing out redundancy notices to its own workers’?”

For Brydon, 61, age has brought a sense of broadening fascination. “I’ve become interested in other things,” he says, “and I love the feeling – and this is going to look awful written down – that I’m evolving.” He speaks of a reverence for nature: birdsong, trees, the feel of his bare feet on the grass. But also for jazz and old cars. “I’m in a very fortunate position,” he says, “to have lots of opportunities to experience new things.”

“That’s the thing,” Coogan says. “Because at a certain level, where we are, we are infantilised. And that can be good and bad. The term ‘behaving like a child’ is double-edged: you can be conceited and selfish, but you can also be curious and open.”

“Which of those would you say you are?” Brydon wonders.

“Sometimes I’m spoilt and I feel like things should just be done for me,” Coogan says. “But I also feel like I’m still able to have a sense of play. Children, when they’re really young, they’re not worried if they’re cool or not, they just do things.” Sometimes, he adds, he looks at politicians young enough to be his own child, and they seem so grown up. “There’s no sense of any playfulness or childlike qualities left in them,” he says, and sighs heavily.

We meet on the day that Nigel Farage is rumoured to be triggering a byelection in his Clacton seat. “Has he resigned?” Brydon asks. “Let’s find out.” He slips into the voice of a TV news anchor. “Steve Coogan is in central London. Steve, what’s the latest on this?”

Coogan checks his phone. “Latest one hour ago. Oh, seven minutes ago. Oh, oh, oh. He’s resigned. He has resigned.” He reads Farage’s statement aloud. “Now, that’s a gamble. A bit like old Burnham’s gamble.”

“Which position will you be taking up in Andy Burnham’s cabinet?” Brydon asks him. In 2025, Coogan was appointed co-chair of the Middleton Mayoral development corporation – a move by Burnham, then still mayor of Greater Manchester, to regenerate the actor’s home town. When Burnham duly campaigned for election in the Makerfield byelection, Coogan joined him on the doorstep. “So what would it be, Defence?” Brydon continues, as Coogan explains his role in Middleton. “Secretary of state for defence, Steve Coogan?”

Coogan bats the idea away. “I am very supportive of him,” he says. “He’s trying to do something really distinctive to get away from Westminster-centric politics. I blame the rise of Reform squarely on what I would call north London intellectual liberals who are part of the cabal of centrist moderation, where they think whether you’re left or right is just an intellectual position, like a game of chess.”

He leans forward in the overstuffed armchair, gathering speed and intensity. “It’s been a game that’s been going on for the last 40 years,” he says. “And people in the provinces, in post-industrial areas, it means nothing to them and nothing has changed. The only relation to working-class people they have is when the plumber comes round. But they have no real empathy for them. And as long as we have people who seem like they’re just a sensible chap, doing a sensible job, Reform will continue to gather momentum because working-class people are fed up, they’re lashing out, they want an alternative, and there are no alternatives around. And that is squarely the fault of the Hampstead Pansies.” He pauses, breathes. “That’s it,” he says.

Brydon describes himself as “probably one of those centrists”. He is not without passion or belief, but when he speaks about his experience of life it is with more contentment than hunger. “I don’t subscribe to more, better, best,” he says. “I feel my role in life is to entertain people.” He talks of how often people approach him to thank him for his work – in Gavin & Stacey, say, or hosting Would I Lie to You? “And I’m very happy with that. I’m happy doing it. And I feel that that is what I put into the world. I try and do good. But I’m not an activist. I’m just not that person.”

It is interesting, then, to think of the young Brydon. The son of a car salesman and a teacher, he grew up in Baglan, near Port Talbot, coming of age at the height of Thatcherism, and just as the nearby steelworks was forced to lay off half its workers. There was certainly something in him that did not want to stick around; like Coogan, he applied, unsuccessfully, to Rada. Surely that shows a dream of something more or better?

“Yes,” he concedes, “in those days, of course. But success came to me later. Steve was successful in his 20s. I was 34, 35, and I had been around the block. I’d had limited success in Wales as a radio and TV personality. And by the time I met Steve, I was making a nice living – ski holidays, two cars, all that stuff – because I was a voice artist. But then it came. So I think I’ve always appreciated it more. I already had three children so I’d matured to a certain degree.”

“The thing Rob has done, what’s not often addressed, is he could have gone down the route of just being a lightweight, fringe act – someone who gets by with getting the stuff that more successful people reject,” Coogan says. “Mopping stuff up, making a living, just getting by by being affable. But, no.” There was a period, he points out, where Brydon was writing and starring in the devastatingly dark comedies Human Remains and Marion & Geoff, and simultaneously making appearances on the Home Shopping network. “The thing I’ve always said to Rob is, he’s a brilliant character actor, but he’s sort of …” he tries to find the most diplomatic way to put it, “… he’s not neglected that, but he’s …”

“Well, I did a bit,” says Brydon. “But when you talk about being content and everything, what no one ever mentions is my five children. When people talk about people’s careers, it’s as if they’re existing in a vacuum. And for me, the choices that I make are because I don’t want to go away. For the last 30 years I’ve had children growing up and the need and the want to be around. So that has been a big part of my career.”

By contrast, Coogan has one daughter, who is now 30. It has been a long time since he was bound by the restrictions of childcare and school holidays. “I do feel like I’m a bit like I’m 24 and have no responsibilities,” he says. “I’ve got a partner, but she has a career, she has another life.”

The divergent paths of their careers is sometimes puzzling to Coogan. He is confused by Brydon’s willingness to be a personality, his ease at being recognised. “You’re so accessible and approachable, they feel like they know you,” he says. Once, the pair walked together up a mountain, and as other walkers approached, Coogan found himself looking away for fear of being recognised. “But he would be face-forward, open and friendly. I would want to avoid that like the plague.” It is easier, sometimes, for him to play a role; Partridge, for example, or even the augmented version of himself we see in The Trip. “Basically, because I don’t feel entirely comfortable in my own skin,” he says.

“That’s the difference,” Brydon interjects. “I do.”

Accordingly, Brydon is quite happy with the span of his career – one week hosting ITV gameshow The Floor, the next playing Peter O’Toole in a Radio 4 drama, followed by “a big animated film” and a new sitcom, Bills Included, for Coogan co-founded production company, Baby Cow. He is never quite sure where the road will take him.

“But the joke I always say is that ‘Steve is driven. I like to be driven. In an S-Class Mercedes or equivalent.’” Coogan laughs. “It was you who said to specify that,” Brydon tells him.

“Well I don’t like people carriers,” Coogan says affably. “The Mercedes – which I wouldn’t drive, but I’d quite like to be a passenger in – is because you can make the rear seat recline. And that’s very important because I like to nap. Now that might sound like I’m a prima donna, but I do like to nap, because I’m 60.”

They joke for a moment about how they are ageing “properly”; a careful balance of somnolence and wonder. I think back to one night in Norway, when Brydon had headed off to bed, and a member of staff rushed in and urged us all to hurry outside. In the cold night air we gathered in the courtyard and looked up. There, high above the silent rooftops, the northern lights undulated across the sky: pale green and pink and golden. I remember how we stood there, quite rapt. And how I looked across at Coogan, and saw his face, lit up like a child. There in the moment, enjoying everything.

The Trip to the Northern Lights starts Thurs 10 December on Sky Atlantic & Now.

GeneralTab.title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
GeneralTab.text:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035

But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.

The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

GeneralTab.title: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
GeneralTab.text:
The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.

Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.

"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".

The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.

GeneralTab.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
GeneralTab.text:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

GeneralTab.title: Job ghosting: What applicants can do if employers do not respond
GeneralTab.text:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."

Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.

The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.

Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview.

"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.

Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.

"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.

GeneralTab.title: Black Friday 2026: Can ChatGPT and other AI tools find you the best bargains?
GeneralTab.text:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035

But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.

The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
articles.text:
The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.

Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.

"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".

The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.

articles.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.text:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

articles.title: Russell Brand's wife says she'll honour prison rules after message row
articles.text:
The wife of disgraced comedian Russell Brand says she will "honour" the rules of his prison, a week after she read a message from her husband proclaiming his innocence.

Laura Brand, 39, drew criticism from ministers after reading out the message from inside HMP Littlehey last week, prompting the government to seek to have the episode removed from social media platforms.

She said on Sunday that she would continue to defend her family and herself over her portrayal in the media during the couple's weekly podcast, which she now presents alone.

Russell Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura Brand said during this week's episode of Sunday Service.

"Now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that."

In the relayed message last week, Russell Brand had said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".

Laura Brand said she had spoken to him at the Cambridgeshire prison and said he was "OK".

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

Further allegations have since been reported about him and some have called for consent laws to be revised.

His conviction has renewed conversation about safeguarding in the media industry, and whether some celebrities are still able to use their fame to prey on women and then silence them.

Ministers have pointed out that inmates are prohibited from making statements that are likely to cause their victims distress and have said Brand's message was being investigated.

A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16, but who was not among the women whose accusations led to his conviction, said his prison message was "upsetting" and "really shocking".

The government attempted to have the podcast removed from YouTube, but this was refused by its owner Google. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged social media companies to "show some decency and take these videos down".

On Sunday, Laura Brand also said that Sunday Service would be a place where she would "continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media's image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny".

She expressed feeling a mixture of "grief", "absence", "desolation" and "loneliness" since her husband's imprisonment.

articles.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
articles.text:
Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".

"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.

But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.

They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".

After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.

Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.

Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.

During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".

Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".

The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.

While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.

She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.

Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.

But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.

"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door.

"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"

The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.

Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.

He remains behind bars awaiting trial.

A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.

"Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away."

"She's doing great for what she's gone through."

They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.

"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

articles.title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
articles.text:
Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.

At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.

In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."

May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.

Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.

The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.

Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.

"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.

"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.

"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.

"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.

"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."

Speaking to the BBC back in 2023, she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".

Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.

May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.

articles.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix result: Max Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collide
articles.text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.

The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.

And in the final laps Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli, and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.

The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.

And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.

Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.

It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines this year.

But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.

The key stories of an engrossing race were:

Verstappen's remarkable intelligence and control in the lead in the most demanding of circumstances

Another dip in a dreadful season for Russell

More controversy at Ferrari, as both drivers earned 10-second penalties for driving infringements in battles involving the other

"How many overtakes did I do?" Verstappen asked his engineer on the slowing down lap, as he reflected on a race the like of which F1 has not seen since the famous Monza slipstreaming battles of the 1960s and early 1970s.

"Yeah, and not many of them on the straight," his new engineer Tom Hart said, summing up how Verstappen had secured the win against the Mercedes challenge.

Lap after lap after lap, Verstappen, who started from pole, would lose the lead to Russell on the Strip only to reclaim it at the last corner, usually going around the outside.

If that did not work, and Russell passed later in the lap, or led across the line, Verstappen developed a trademark move around the outside of Turn Three to get back in front.

The race went on and on like that, punctuated by a mid-grand prix safety car, but through it all Verstappen always seemed in control.

As the race wore on, Antonelli came into the picture after starting sixth, and passed Russell with 12 laps to go to become Verstappen's main challenger.

Now it was the Italian's turn to swap places with Verstappen, but again the Dutchman had the measure of Mercedes.

At one point, Verstappen asked his team to come up with a better deployment strategy for the final lap because he thought Mercedes had "figured it out".

They came back to him to say that he had already come up with the best approach.

In the end, though, he need not have worried, as his rivals behind him gave him enough of a gap at the start of the final lap to not have to worry too much about defending his lead.

That critical final phase started with Russell deciding to make a move to become Verstappen's challenger again.

Russell went for a move into Turn Five with two laps to go but he locked up his brakes over the bumps heading into the corner - bumps that had earlier taken Red Bull's Isack Hadjar out of the lead battle when his front wing broke over them - and went straight on into the barrier.

Russell managed to reverse out of the barrier, but a ninth-place finish was not what he was expecting.

The incident was also unfortunate for him in the context of his calling out Verstappen's driving after qualifying, when he said "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

Verstappen had the last word, both on track and literally. After seeing Russell's embarrassing mistake, Verstappen came on the radio to say: "Hah, hah. Well done. My God."

Now Antonelli looked to be the man who would challenge Verstappen for the win.

But that was counting without the McLarens. Piastri had already driven an outstanding race to recover from starting 17th because of an engine penalty and Norris had at one point dropped out of the top 10 in the chaotic lead battle in the first part of the grand prix.

But they were third and fourth around the penultimate lap and both swept around Antonelli around the outside of the fast final corner heading into the last lap.

Antonelli had lifted off the throttle because he wanted to stay behind Verstappen and attack him later, but in so doing had triggered a setting in the engine defined by the rules that left him without battery power.

It deprived him of the chance to deploy what Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff said was a "secret" deployment strategy on the final lap that he felt would have kept Antonelli ahead through the final corners after passing Verstappen down the Strip.

Instead, it gave Verstappen breathing space, and Antonelli was delayed sufficiently that he could not recover to challenge them.

Second-placed Norris summed it up, saying: "I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1. I didn't know what was happening half the time."

articles.title: EU deal: 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
articles.text:
"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

Burnham promised a "brainstorm" on stage in Brussels yesterday, so what's his plan?

The prime minister's precise message on Europe is, maybe characteristically, not that precise.

From the by-election platform in the summer where he promised not to reopen old arguments and emphasised he was not proposing the UK considers rejoining, to telling the BBC the country could "go all the way" and go back in, to now the promises of a "national conversation" and "brainstorm" with the EU - his words have varied over time.

No 10 plainly wants to move closer to the EU, even if ministers suggest there really is no end fixed position and so this period of working it out is genuine.

They tell me that, in private, "Andy is pretty clearly where he is publicly - he does think it's a big discussion we have to have as a country, it's a national discussion in the context of the 10 year plan, but also has to involve the Europeans".

In other words, even though he makes no secret that he'd like to be in the EU and wishes we had never left, the prime minister won't conclude whether he'll promise to take the country back in until he has a better idea of what relationship he might get out of the EU - and, perhaps too, how the public responds.

Two quick reminders: Burnham has said it wouldn't happen before another election; and, remember there are elections in Europe too. This whole conversation might be transformed if Marine Le Pen becomes the president of France, or the march of other parties who are suspicious of Brussels continues.

The prime minister's body language in Brussels yesterday, though, and his proclamation that it was a "good day" for Britain, displays happiness in government at what they have achieved so far - closer ties on food exports, energy, and allowing young people to live and work more freely on both sides of the Channel.

Despite a last minute classic spanner in the works with a lack of agreement on tuition fees, the UK side feels positive they didn't back down on that issue yesterday, and the broader deals were concluded anyway.

And despite the protestations from the foreign secretary that the deals will all come into force whatever happens on fees, the government will start the legal processes to turn the agreements into law - although there are still plenty of opportunities for other countries to try and unpick them further down the track.

Of course, politicians' reactions to the deal depend which side they were on in the Brexit debate.

The Lib Dems, SNP, Greens and Plaid Cymru plead the case that it's not far enough. The Conservatives complain it's not fair, for example, that British farmers will have to follow EU rules to make life easier for those who trade with the bloc. Reform scream it's a betrayal of the 2016 vote.

But the feeling in government is the summit was a success and showed the EU will allow the UK to pick and choose where to cooperate, and is willing to listen to what the prime minister wants to do next. It's worth saying just as in any negotiation, the EU might always be up for giving if it receives in return.

Yet as May warns, doing deals with the European Union is simply, a long hard slog.

And one senior Whitehall source cautions the prime minister not to kid himself that an early feel-good factor doesn't mean future haggling would be a doddle: "British prime ministers can be oddly delusional about the EU - they can get seduced by the hope that good relationships with individual leaders will overcome the ideological inertia in Brussels which is overseen by French and German lawyerly high priests and priestesses.

"European leaders might actually be your friends, but they are not the ones in charge of decision-making in Brussels."

And a former negotiator warns that in his "brainstorm," the prime minister might well find the deal he's concluded this week just about rubs up against the limits of what can be done without going for the full-fat option - telling me: "There isn't much more to go with a strategy of incrementally building on the deal before it becomes quite a binary choice."

They add a reality check for any deal-making with the EU: "The EU have a very set way of doing things, that is more about their own unity than about who they are negotiating with."

Then of course, there is the politics at home. When cornered on this subject the prime minister and his cabinet often say the "British people will be the boss" - going on to cite polling that clearly displays disappointment with Brexit and a discernible interest in going back in.

But that's not the same as polling suggesting the public is demanding the government puts it at the top of the list.

As one senior Labour figure puts it, there has "certainly been a shift - and an openness to have the conversation" about rejoining, but the PM "has to be really careful about locking himself into a manifesto commitment that alienates a lot of people" alongside plenty of voters who might welcome a move.

What of May's warnings about getting tangled up in EU talks at the exclusion of all else?

One government insider from the time asks: "Can you even remember anything else that happened between 2017 and 2020? It's extremely naïve to think he can do all the other things that are extremely pressing, like defence, or Neets, while trying to play out a future with the EU - it won't happen."

It's worth noting, as some ministers do privately, that Burnham himself was not working in Westminster during the most intense struggles over leaving the EU - an advantage perhaps, that he doesn't carry that baggage, or a gap in his experience of how bad it was.

And yet, the prime minister - who, crucially, is confident in his ability to communicate with the public - is plainly resolved on exploring going back into the European Union, and choosing to take that argument on.

After what the government considers to have been a successful summit, that adventure looks more tempting to the many in Labour's tribe who think he is right to do exactly that.

After the last 72 hours, opportunity is knocking - but the warnings from prime ministers past ring out too.

Under May, Brexit affected nearly everyone and everything - trying to go back in under Burnham could perhaps affect everyone and everything too.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.text:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.

Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.

The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.text:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
articles.text:
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.
